summary:
Western Sahara is a disputed territory under Moroccan military administration. Where Moroccan security services operate, a visitor stands under Morocco's penal code, including its morality provisions, and before Moroccan courts. Human Rights Watch's dispatch of 9 December 2005 records that legal framework in practice: seven human-rights defenders from Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara were tried on charges of fomenting illegal protests, charges the organisation called dubious, and Sahrawi activists were detained by Moroccan security services.

Same-sex intimacy is criminalised, with the sources on record setting the maximum penalty at three years' imprisonment. The broad discretion police hold in applying morality provisions is the instrument turned on visibly trans people. Rights reviews document involuntary outing of trans people, discrepancies in how a person may present at checkpoints and in registry records, and an absence of any trans-specific legal protection.

The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, a partially recognised state and African Union member since 2016, claims sovereignty over Western Sahara and separately records homosexuality as illegal for men and women and as illegal there for decades. A July 2017 global legality roundup lists it as a criminalising jurisdiction, and the Council for Global Equality, Equaldex and ILGA all record same-sex sexual activity as illegal for both males and females there, punishable by up to three years. Both claimed frameworks record criminalisation, and neither supplies a defence for a visibly trans visitor.

No protection against discrimination or violence is recorded on either side. The Spanish Commission for Refugee Aid (CEAR) states that no type of protection exists for LGBTQ individuals in case of discrimination or violence. In 2010 Ahmed Mulay Alli, the claimant government's diplomatic representative in Mexico, said its constitution does not refer to homosexuality or any other sexual practice and does not punish it, which CEAR concludes leaves no legal protection against discrimination or violence.
tangentialFactors:
Morocco, which occupies most of the territory the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic claims, also criminalises same-sex activity, so the criminalising position is shared across both claimed authorities rather than contested between them.

The legal inheritance of the territory runs through Spanish colonial rule, which ended in 1976, and homosexuality was not decriminalised in Spain until 1979. The territory therefore took independence from a colonial power that had not itself removed the offence.

The 2005 prosecution of the seven human-rights defenders indicates the due-process climate a visitor's case would enter: charges characterised by Human Rights Watch as dubious, tried before Moroccan courts, with security services exercising authority in the territory.

A 2009 United States Committee for Refugees and Immigrants (USCRI) report found that Sahrawi government officials running refugee camps in Algeria said they were holding some prisoners on homosexuality charges even while alleging facts that would more fittingly describe rape. The charge is applied to conduct the officials themselves describe as coercive, which points to arbitrary and mislabelled detention under the morality provisions.

Most residents of the territory are Muslim and same-sex relationships are seen as a foreign phenomenon. That social setting raises the cost of visible gender nonconformity beyond the statutory penalty, for a visitor as much as for a resident.
localsOnly:
Residents hold no statutory protection against discrimination or violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. CEAR records the absence explicitly and ties it to the claimant government's constitutional silence, which its diplomatic representative confirmed publicly in 2010.

Registry records and personal presentation are documented points of exposure for trans residents: rights reviews record discrepancies between how a person presents and how they are recorded, and involuntary outing as a consequence of those discrepancies, including at checkpoints.

Residents of the refugee camps in Algeria fall under the claimant government's administration, where officials reported in 2009 holding prisoners on homosexuality charges. The charge there has been used against conduct the officials themselves described as resembling rape.

Same-sex relationships are widely regarded as a foreign import in the territory's social setting, so visible nonconformity carries stigma that operates independently of whether a court charges anyone.
outOfScopeNotes:
The lower bound of the penalty is unresolved. The record on file states a maximum of three years' imprisonment but does not corroborate a six-month minimum, so the full sentencing range should be verified against the operative penal text before it is quoted.

Whether Morocco's penal code extends to the territory by statute or only by the reach of its security services is not sourced here. The inventory establishes that Moroccan courts and security services exercise authority in the territory, not the instrument of extension.

No trans-specific statutory provision is sourced for either claimed framework. The trans risk documented in the record rests on enforcement practice under general morality provisions and on registry and checkpoint handling, not on a named gender-identity offence.

The claimant government's constitutional text is quoted only through a 2010 diplomatic statement; the full text and its definitions are not verified in this inventory. The 2017 roundup status and the ILGA, Equaldex and Council for Global Equality entries are secondary compilations.

Visa, entry and border-screening procedures for the territory are not sourced in this inventory, so whether a trans visitor's documents are examined at the point of entry remains unresolved. No incident of violence against a trans visitor with a date and outcome is documented here.
